summary: An island nation at the eastern edge of the Caribbean, formerly a British colony, independent in 1966 and a republic since 2021, known for sugarcane, rum and tourism.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism arrived with the English colonization of Barbados in 1627. The Anglican Church was the official church in the colonial period, the sugar plantation owners were mostly Anglican, and the island was divided into 11 parishes, which are still the administrative divisions today. From the 18th century the Moravian Brethren and the Methodists preached to the slaves, and after emancipation in 1834 the Anglican Church also actively took in African-descended believers; in the 20th century Pentecostals and Seventh-day Adventists grew, so that Protestants overall make up about two-thirds of the population.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown in recent decades to about 20%, mainly among urban younger generations. Barbados has a very high rate of education and close ties with Britain and North America, so it has been influenced by Western secularization; at the same time, the Anglican Church lost its status as the state church in 1969 and the role of the church in public life has gradually weakened.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was long restricted during the British colonial period; in the early colonial years Irish Catholics mostly came to Barbados as indentured laborers or exiles and had a low status. Only in the late 19th century did the Catholic Church formally develop on the island, and today its followers make up about 4%, some of them immigrants from neighboring islands and Latin America.

ranking.name: Other (Islam, Hinduism, etc.)
ranking.description: Other religions include Islam, Hinduism and Judaism. Most Hindus and Muslims are descendants of merchants who moved from Gujarat in India and from Guyana in the 20th century; Jews came to Barbados from Brazil as early as the 1650s, and the Nidhe Israel Synagogue in Bridgetown, built around 1654, is one of the oldest synagogues in the Western Hemisphere.

religion.background: Barbados had no indigenous settlers before English colonization in 1627, and the colonists brought in large numbers of West African slaves to develop sugar cultivation, making Barbados one of Britain's richest colonies in the 17th century. The Anglican Church was the state church in the colonial period, while the Moravian Brethren and Methodists preached to the slaves in the 18th century. After emancipation in 1834, African-descended residents joined the Protestant churches in large numbers, and church schools became an important channel of social mobility. After independence in 1966, the Anglican Church lost its status as state church in 1969, religion became more diverse, and in recent years the non-religious population has also gradually increased.

ranking.name: English (including Barbadian Creole, Bajan)
ranking.description: English arrived with English colonization in 1627. Barbados was a British colony until independence in 1966 and was therefore nicknamed 'Little England'; the government, education and media use standard English. In daily life most people speak Barbadian Creole (Bajan), which formed in the plantation era from a mixture of the languages of West African slaves and the dialects of southwestern England, and whose grammar bears the features of West African languages.

ranking.name: Other (Hindustani and other immigrant languages)
ranking.description: The other languages were mainly brought by immigrants of the 20th century and include Indian languages such as Gujarati and Hindi, as well as the languages used by Indo-Guyanese immigrants from Guyana. In recent years immigrants from Venezuela and other Latin American countries have also brought Spanish, but the speakers of these languages total only about 2%.

language.history: The indigenous Arawaks and Caribs of Barbados had already left the island by the time the English arrived, so no indigenous language has survived. From 1627 the English colonized the island, and the large numbers of West African slaves on the plantations came into contact with English and Irish indentured laborers, forming Barbadian Creole. Barbados is one of Britain's earliest colonies in the Caribbean and one that never changed hands, so English cultural influence has been especially deep. After independence in 1966 English remained the official language, and in recent years Barbados has also moved to treat Bajan as a national cultural heritage.

ranking.name: Cou-cou and flying fish
ranking.description: A smooth cornmeal porridge (cou-cou) stirred and cooked with okra, served with flying fish steamed in a sauce of tomato, onion and spices, the national dish of Barbados.
ranking.history: The way of making cou-cou derives from the corn-and-okra food tradition brought by West African slaves and is similar to West African cornmeal porridges. Flying fish are abundant in the waters around Barbados, which is therefore called the 'Land of the Flying Fish', and a flying fish even appears on Barbadian coins. This national dish often appears on family tables on Fridays and Saturdays, showing the combination of African tradition and island produce.

ranking.name: Pudding and souse
ranking.description: A steamed pudding made of sweet potato mash stuffed into pig intestine, served with slices of pork pickled in lime juice, onion and chili (souse), mingling sour and spicy.
ranking.history: This dish originates from the plantation era, when slaves were often given lesser parts such as pig's head, feet and intestines, and so made pudding from sweet potato and spices and pickled the pork in lime juice. Sweet potato is a common Caribbean crop, while lime and chili were used for seasoning and preservation. Today pudding and souse is the traditional Saturday meal of Barbados, and many small eateries serve this dish only on Saturdays.

ranking.name: Macaroni pie
ranking.description: Macaroni is mixed with cheese, eggs, milk, mustard and ketchup and baked, then cut into squares to eat, with a firm texture and a rich cheese flavor.
ranking.history: Macaroni pie shares its origin with British macaroni cheese, and the method was introduced to Barbados during British colonial times. Unlike the creamy-sauce macaroni and cheese of North America, the Barbadian version is baked until set so that it can be cut into blocks, and mustard and ketchup are added for flavor. It is an essential side dish at Barbadian Sunday family lunches, often served with rice and peas, fried chicken or roast meat.

ranking.name: Conkies
ranking.description: Cornmeal, pumpkin, sweet potato, coconut, raisins and spices are mixed, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed, giving a moist texture with coconut aroma and sweetness.
ranking.history: Conkies derive from the leaf-wrapped steamed food tradition brought by West African slaves and are similar to Ghana's 'kenkey' and Antigua's ducana. In Barbados they are closely tied to Independence Day on November 30 (independence in 1966) and are traditionally made around Independence Day. In the past they were also eaten on 'Guy Fawkes Night' (November 5) in the British colonial period, but now they have mainly become the symbolic food of Independence Day.

ranking.name: Fish cakes
ranking.description: Salt cod is soaked in water to remove the salt and shredded, then mixed with flour, onion, herbs and chili into a batter, scooped into small portions and fried into golden balls, crisp outside and soft inside.
ranking.history: Fish cakes are related to the Caribbean salt-fish food tradition: in the 17th–18th centuries merchants from New England and Canada traded salt cod for Barbados's sugar and rum, and salt fish became an important protein source for plantation slaves. Today fish cakes are the most popular snack in Barbados, often tucked into the local 'salt bread' rolls, called 'bread and two', a common snack at breakfast and parties.
